T11 stays stopped. Nothing restarts until you say so.

**The update.** The PA3 release that adds external coders already looks installed: it's the newest commit, 682d3e76af. If you meant a newer release, the mod will offer it in its own picker. If you meant a status update on the work, here's where T11 was when it paused on the 17th:
- **Committed:** 78 functions cracked, in two batches, both 218/218 byte-identical.
- **Not started:** 27 batches, 246 functions. 14 of those batches are routed Haiku-first.
- **Haiku's walls:** 18 functions Haiku couldn't crack still need their Opus retry.

**Your setup worked.** I ran the check, and all three configs connect:

| Config | Model | Check |
|---|---|---|
| openrouter-deepseek | deepseek | connected |
| openrouter-glm | glm | connected |
| openrouter-qwen | qwen3 | connected |

None of them is set up for this project yet. There's no default coder, no lanes and no escalation rule, so nothing uses them until we decide.

**How these differ from what T11 tried.** T11's "external lane" was a custom script, `.run/P40/T11/ext/lane.py`. It made the model draft a function through the API in one go. DeepSeek ran 9 of its 28 functions that way, cracked none, and spent $0.21. The new external coders are different. Each is our own coder agent with the full toolset (it can read, edit, compile, compare the bytes and try again), just running on DeepSeek, GLM or Qwen. That's a much fairer test than the old lane gave them. Their tokens cost cash on your OpenRouter keys, not subscription usage.

**What PA3's own tests found:**
- **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash:** the recommended model. It's the cheapest, and max effort helps on hard work.
- **GLM 5.3 Flash:** about 3 times DeepSeek's price. Most of its hardest attempts ran out of time, its hosts were unreliable, and it needs max effort even on easy tasks.
- **Qwen 3.8 Flash:** passed nearly everything it finished, but at 6 to 11 times DeepSeek's price per task, because its only host barely caches.

**My recommendation: a small bake-off inside T11.** T11 is a good test bed. Every function is independent, the byte check decides whether a crack is right, and wrong code can't get in because every win goes through the same committer and the 218/218 check. Here's what I'd do:
- **One batch each.** DeepSeek, GLM and Qwen each get one of the unstarted Haiku-first batches, about 8 to 10 functions each, at max effort. That compares them with Haiku's 57% on functions of the same kind.
- **Walls go to Opus.** Anything an external coder can't crack goes to an Opus retry, the same rule Haiku's walls follow. Escalation is set to in-house.
- **Everything else stays as it is.** Haiku-first for the other batches, and Opus for the large functions and those with more than one kind of lever.
- **The old lane retires.** Its 9 results stay in the comparison table.
- **The summary compares them.** T11's summary gets a row per model: crack rate, minutes and dollars per crack.

Then we'd decide on real numbers whether one of them takes over the cracking work in later phases.

Three things to settle:
- **Your 4-coder cap.** Do external coders count toward it, or run on top of it? They don't spend subscription usage, but they do add compile load on this machine. Also, disk space was about 6 GB the last time I checked.
- **A credit limit on each key.** Please confirm each key has one, plus a guardrail at openrouter.ai that allows only the recommended host. Without the guardrail, OpenRouter spreads requests over many hosts, some pricier and some serving lower-quality copies of the model.
- **T11's resume note.** On resume, the expert should read the note T11 committed when it paused (in 1a0eea2f4b). The mod has since overwritten that file with a thinner recovery note. I'll point the expert at the committed one.

Pick an option in the picker. Once you've chosen, I'll write the project settings and a three-line "External coders" section on the card. When you say go, I'll pass the routing to T11's expert as it resumes.

My recommendation is to keep banking on the in-house Opus coder, as T11 already does. It costs little, and it's the one step where a mistake hurts the whole wave.

**What banking is.** One coder takes the finished batches' wins and puts them into the real source tree. It rewrites the matching residue rows, re-runs the type census and the cast check, runs the full 218/218 build check and commits. So it's the single point where everyone's work meets the shared tree.

**Why Opus there:**
- **It's a small share of the tokens.** Batch 1's banker used about 78k tokens, against about 2.7M for the crack coders so far, so about 3%. Moving it to DeepSeek would save very little.
- **It's where an error costs most.** A bad crack only wastes one function's attempt. A bad bank can stall the wave: a broken merge, a wrongly rewritten residue row, or a commit that leaves the tree red. Batch 2 hit just such a snag. The census had to be re-run before the cast sweep after the function bodies were swapped, and an Opus coder caught it.
- **It's judgment work, not repetitive work.** That fits your rule: DeepSeek does the bulk per-function cracking, and in-house coders do the rest.

**One cheap improvement: bank less often.** Each bank pays for a full 218/218 run, about half an hour of machine time. With 27 batches left, I'd bank every 6 to 8 finished batches instead of every 4, so about 4 banks in all. That cuts the gate runs and the banker's tokens further. The risk is small, because every win sits in scratch, already byte-checked one function at a time, until it's banked.

There's also a middle option, if you want to see how DeepSeek copes: let it bank one batch while Opus does the rest, and compare. I wouldn't start there, though. Let's first see how it cracks.

If you agree, I'll add "bank every 6 to 8 batches" to T11's resume instructions. T11 is still stopped until you say go.

Partly. The expert decides when to bank and writes the instructions, but a coder does the banking itself. For batch 1, the expert filled in its banking template (`.run/P40/T11/bank_brief.txt`) and spawned a coder, T11.c101, which made commit 8408af290c. Batch 2 went the same way, as T11.c102.

The reason is a house rule: an expert does a job itself only when it fits in about 10 tool calls, and anything with an edit, build and test loop goes to a coder. Banking is well beyond that:
- swap each cracked body into its source file;
- rewrite the matching residue rows;
- re-run the type census and the cast check;
- run the full 218/218 build check, which takes about half an hour;
- commit.

It also keeps the expert's own context small for the many hours of the wave.

A coder also doesn't bank each time it returns a match. Matches wait in scratch, already byte-checked one function at a time, and the expert banks a few batches' worth together. That way, one 218/218 run covers many wins.

So my earlier advice stands. The coder the expert sends to bank stays on in-house Opus, and the expert could bank every 6 to 8 batches to save gate runs. T11 is still stopped until you say go.

Adding a model is a setup you run yourself, in a normal terminal. Don't run it through `!` here: it asks for your key with hidden typing, and anything typed in this chat stays in the conversation log.

The steps:
1. **Create a key** at openrouter.ai and give it a credit limit. If the new model's best host differs from DeepSeek's, use a new key just for this model, because a key's guardrail covers every model on it.
2. **Run the setup** in a WSL terminal, since the project runs in WSL:
   `sh ~/.claude/pa3-src/project-architect-3.0/setup-external.sh`
   It asks for:
   - the URL: press Enter for OpenRouter;
   - a name for the config, for example `openrouter-<model>`;
   - the key;
   - the model id, copied from the model's OpenRouter page in the form `vendor/model`.

   It tests the model and saves nothing if the test fails.
3. **Add the guardrail.** The setup lists the model's hosts, best first, and names the recommended one. Add a guardrail on the key at openrouter.ai that allows only that host.

Your next message here will bring me the setup's result. I'll run the connection check then, and we'll decide what the new model is for. Today all function cracking goes to DeepSeek, so the new model could replace it, split the batches with it for a comparison, or wait for a later wave.

Which model is it? If you tell me now, I can look up what PA3's tests or OpenRouter's page say about its price and its hosts while you run the setup. T11 is still stopped.

**One thing you should know first.** The model id the setup saved is `minimax/minimax-m3.1-flash:free`, the free variant. Two catches come with free models on OpenRouter:
- **Rate limits.** Free variants get a small number of requests per minute and per day. A cracking coder makes hundreds of calls per function, so 4 coders will probably hit the limit. Runs may then fail with 429 errors and pile up on your held list, even though the model could have cracked those functions. PA3 also hasn't tested MiniMax, so I have no crack rate to compare it with.
- **Prompt logging.** Free endpoints typically log prompts and may train on them. A coder's prompts include our source and the game's disassembly from `asm/`, which is ROM-derived and which we deliberately keep out of the public repo.

If you meant the paid version, run the setup again with the id without `:free`. Then the credit limit caps the spending, as before. If the free variant is deliberate, it works as configured. Expect slow or failing runs under load, and watch the held list early.

PA3 has a new build of 3.30, the release that adds external coders. It brings these changes:

- **External coders, finished.** Coding can run on a cheaper model through OpenRouter, while experts, retrievers, the planner and I stay on Claude. They run at high effort unless you ask for another. An external coder is our own coder on your key, with the same rules. Its card shows the model and its steps. A run cut off by a restart picks up where it stopped. A failed run goes to an in-house coder by default, but your rule in this project holds MiniMax's failures for you instead.
- **The spend is visible.** Once the first external coder starts, the statusline shows `External · tokens · $ spent · $ left`. A free model like your MiniMax variant shows $0.
- **The band shows them as coders.** An external coder appears as `pa-coder T11 · c<n>` with its model and latest step. The session's token count includes what external coders read.
- **PA3 learns from each run.** A finished external coder's report lists the commands it was refused and other friction. The expert proposes fixes, and I'll ask you before anything is kept: an allow rule for this project, or a note that later coders get.
- **Cancelled tasks stay cancelled.** If you cancel a stopped task, or put it back in the queue, it's no longer restarted when work goes on. The loop starts the plan's next task instead.

The mod's own files changed in this update, and a setting changed that only takes effect after a restart. So please restart Claude Code. No task starts until then, and you'll pick up where you left off. That includes T11, which resumes with MiniMax doing the cracking. I sent the routing to its expert before the update.

Yes, it kept going, but it didn't decide that itself. The launcher that runs external coders sent the "go on" message.

**What happened.** The launcher (`tools/pa_ext.py`) checks that a coder's final message starts with the bare word "done", "question" or "blocked". If it doesn't, the launcher assumes the coder stopped too early and nudges it with "Go on with the task". G07's report began "All deliverables are in place. Here is my report." and only then said "done". So the launcher nudged it, and G07 read the nudge as a go and started a new function, func_801415C0. That's a gap in PA3's check: the report was really done.

**What I've done.** I've told T11's expert to:
- **Stop G07 now.** Its paused-on function was already finished and recorded, with 2 matches and 1 wall. It drops the new function's scratch and leaves that function marked as never attempted.
- **Warn every coder.** Each coder's final message must start with the bare word, with nothing before it, so the launcher doesn't nudge them on again.
- **Log it as a known harness quirk.** It goes in T11's log.

The other three coders (G06, G08 and G10) received the pause and are finishing their current functions. I'll tell you when everything is idle and you can restart.

**The lever that cracked both headers:** the pins were masking a wrong prototype. The tree spells the shared header `void func_8012EF34(s32, s32)`, but the game's real function returns `s32` — 5 TUs already declare it `extern s32` and consume the value, and `src/ov_SC01_084/ov_SC01_084_jr_80182A00.c` carries a warning that the `void` spelling leaks the return value. Restoring the `s32` prototype keeps `$v0` live across the `gte_stsz` asm, so local-alloc can no longer hand `$v0` to the `&sp10`/reload temp and gives it `$v1` ($3) — exactly the register the two `register ... __asm__("$3")` pins were forcing. The bodies are lever-free (plain `s32 r` returned; no `register`, no `__asm__`). Verified: score 0 on 141/141 includers for each header, and the whole-object bank verdict IDENTICAL on every recipe.

**func_800D02D0** stays a WALL: the target loads `D_800D3768[arg0].word0` into `$v1` and keeps the `&D_800C7C60` pointer in `$v0`; lever-free `p` makes the *load* take `$v0` instead, because `p` becomes a global pseudo live across the `func_8001ABBC` call and global-alloc gives it `$v3` while the local keeps `$v2`. Best 8 of 39 tries.

**For the expert's judgement on the two MATCHes:** 1294 TUs declare `extern void func_8012EF34(s32, s32)` and 5 declare `extern s32`. The header is the definition the 136 including TUs compile against; the 1299 call sites' compiled bytes are unaffected (the callee ABI is unchanged — the flag still leaves in `$v0`), and the 5 value-consuming sites were already declaring `s32` and reading `$v0`. If you prefer the header to stay `void`, both items become WALLs instead, and the 5 value-consuming callers remain the status-quo inconsistency rather than a regression.

T21 should now run before T11. The first attempt didn't work because of a gap in PA3, so I worked around it.

**The gap.** My plan changes don't land while a task is stopped. Queued changes only land when the loop reaches a task boundary, and T11's stop isn't one. So the new task, and the move putting it before T11, were sitting in the queue. Some older change-log lines were stuck too, from the 17th and from earlier today, because T11 has been running since then with no boundary.

**What I did:**
- **Put T11 back in line myself.** I ran the plan tool directly to set T11 to "queued" (T11 isn't running) and committed it. Normally only the mod runs that tool for me. I made this one exception because the queue couldn't move any other way.
- **Released T11's stop.** Because the plan now has T11 queued, the mod drops it instead of resuming it. The loop then reaches a boundary, where every queued change lands in order: the stuck change-log lines (including the MiniMax routing), the new cookbook task T21, and T21 moved to the front.
- **Released the talk hold.**

T21 should start next, and T11 resumes after it. The commit also picked up the journal and T11's coder logs that were waiting in the tree, which is harmless. If the mod refuses anything, or T11 starts instead, I'll tell you. This gap is worth reporting as a PA3 bug: a plan change has no way to land while a task is stopped.

This is the local-alloc for block-confined pseudos. The key: "Only the pseudos that die but once can be handled" — local-alloc handles a pseudo whose live range is within one basic block and which dies once. It assigns regs by "qty" (quantities) and the priority ordering.

Hmm. So how did the asm break it? Because the asm's output is a hard REG, and cse cannot rewrite an asm's input operand. So the first use's value comes from the asm (a reg), and the second use is the plain expression → not unified.

- A value produced by an asm — banned.
- A value from a *function call* — no.
- A **volatile** load — no.
- A value computed from an unknown-but-equal expression: e.g. `p1 = sp10 + 4;` where sp10 is a *pointer to a pointer*? no.

```
__asm__ volatile("" : "=r"(v0) : "0"(v0), "m"(pad));
```
This is a "REFUSED launder with 2 inputs" — a volatile asm with an output tied to the input v0 and a memory input "m"(pad). The "m"(pad) input makes it a *memory* reference (pad is a local!) → the asm forces `pad` to be *addressed* (it's in the frame) and forces the asm to be kept (volatile).

So this lever does two things: (a) makes v0 opaque, (b) forces the local `pad` to have an address (i.e. the frame must reserve space for it) — the "pad" local is a *frame pad*!

It's the third: cracking to remove register pins and inline asm. It isn't about structs, and it isn't for fun. One update first: the cookbook task T21 finished at 17:33. It added four new cookbook entries (C0530 to C0533) and either filed or ruled out the rest. T11 then picked up again with MiniMax.

**Why there are pins at all.** To reach 100% matched, every function had to compile to exactly the same bytes as the retail game. When plain C wouldn't quite produce those bytes, agents used "levers", which force the compiler's hand:
- **Register pins:** `register int x asm("$16")` tells the compiler which CPU register a variable must live in.
- **Inline asm:** raw machine instructions written straight into the C.
- **Compiler barriers:** tricks that stop the compiler from moving or merging code.

They work, but they're tech debt. A human reader sees assembly tricks instead of C, and the code only builds the same way on this exact compiler. The original programmers at Square wrote plain C. So for nearly every pinned function, some plain-C spelling exists that the compiler turns into the same bytes. It just wasn't found yet.

**What "cracking" means here.** Taking a function that already matches with levers and finding a lever-free C version that still compiles to identical bytes. Coders try different spellings: a different variable type, a different statement order, a variable reused instead of a new one. Each try is compiled and compared byte for byte until one matches with no levers. Today's feed shows one: G07's coder cracked `func_8003DF8C` by declaring two loop counters as `u16` instead of `int`. That changed how the compiler handled their copies, and the pin was no longer needed.

**Why "singleton".** Earlier tasks cleared the cheap cases:
- **T7** turned many pins into missing function parameters, which they really were.
- **T8** removed the levers that turned out not to be needed at all.
- **T9** cracked the 38 "head classes": groups where the same lever appears in many functions, so cracking one example fixed every copy.

What's left are singletons: functions whose lever appears nowhere else, about 400 of them. No fix carries over from another function, so each one has to be cracked by itself. That's why T11 is a "wave" of many coders working through batches of 8 to 10 functions.

**Why it matters.** The goal of this generation of phases is legible source: plain C with real types and names, not just matching bytes. The milestone you set for this phase is that every lever is either removed or has a recorded reason, the specific compiler behaviour that plain C can't reproduce (its "wall"). So every cracked function becomes clean C, and every function that won't crack gets its wall written down instead of staying a mystery. The struct work you're thinking of is separate. That was T2 to T5, and T17 comes later.

The queue was held while we talked, and I'm releasing it now.

With T21 done and T11 resumed, I should explain in plain terms: a lever is something like pinned registers or inline asm or compiler hints used to force byte-for-byte matching output. A singleton lever is one whose exact text appears in only one function, so fixing it doesn't require propagating changes elsewhere. The underlying goal is clean, legible pure-C source — levers represent technical debt, and the milestone is reached once every lever is either removed or explicitly documented against a named compiler quirk; this isn't related to struct layout.

PA3 has a small fix release, 3.30.2. It's about how updates behave when a session starts:

- **An update now always tells you to restart.** If PA3 updated itself while a session was starting, that session used to say the new release was loaded and carry on, even though it was still running the old code. Now the session knows it's on the old code. The statusline shows the install in progress, and when the install finishes I'll tell you to restart and start no work until you do.
- **A silent update check gets reported.** If the start-of-session update check gets no answer in time, I'll tell you in one line. Before, the statusline's "checking for updates" just disappeared.
- **Internal test changes.** PA3's own tests were adjusted for a change in Claude Code's test kit. Nothing changes in your sessions.

This session already runs 3.30.2, so you don't need to restart for it.

**Project Architect 3.30.2 is installed and loaded. Ready to continue work.**

T11 is starting fresh with a new expert, using one MiniMax coder at first.

The new expert has these instructions:
- **It starts from the committed resume note** (d37317858e) and each batch's handoff.
- **It runs one external coder at first,** on one paused batch of 5 functions or fewer. PA3 3.30.1 would hold a model new to the project to one coder at a time anyway, until one of its runs comes back clean.
- **The judge rules on commands no allow rule covers.** PA3's judge runs on Opus with auto mode's rules. It decides each such command once, and the project remembers the decision. The expert won't pre-approve anything to get around it, so we'll see the judge make real decisions.
- **It reviews that coder's report before spawning anything else.** It looks at:
  - which commands were refused or judged;
  - the friction the coder hit;
  - what worked.

  Then it fixes its next brief, writes notes for later external coders and adds new crack moves to the cookbook. Each note comes to you as a one-line FYI with its undo, and nothing waits on you.
- **Then it scales up,** to the usual 4 MiniMax coders, resuming the remaining batches from their handoffs.

The rest of the routing hasn't changed:
- An in-house Opus coder banks the wins every 6 to 8 finished batches.
- Walls and failed runs go on your held list.
- func_8012EF34 and func_8012EF70 are still waiting on your ruling.
- Every coder is reminded to begin its final message with the bare word "done", so the launcher doesn't nudge it into another function.

I've released the talk hold too. If the mod refuses either release, I'll tell you.

T11 is the singleton crack wave. It takes about 400 functions that already compile to the retail bytes only with "levers" and tries to rewrite each one in plain C that still compiles to the same bytes. Levers are register pins, inline asm and compiler barriers that force the compiler's output. They're called singletons because each function's lever appears nowhere else, so no fix from another function carries over and each one is cracked by itself. A function that won't crack gets its "wall" recorded instead, meaning the compiler behaviour plain C can't reproduce. That's this phase's milestone: every lever is either removed or has its reason written down.

Right now the new expert has started a single MiniMax coder, T11.cG08c, as you asked. It's picking up batch G08b, which has 4 functions left. The expert gave it no pre-approved commands, so any command no rule covers goes to PA3's judge, and the expert will review those decisions in the coder's report. Once the expert has gone through that report and adjusted its brief, it scales up to 4 coders on the remaining batches. An Opus coder banks the cracks every 6 to 8 finished batches.

Partly. The batches are grouped by lever type, but cracking one function doesn't mean the coder can crack the others the same way.

**Why one crack doesn't carry over.** These are singletons: each function's lever appears nowhere else. The functions that shared the exact same lever were already handled in T9, where cracking one example fixed every copy. So in T11 there's no exact fix to copy from one function to the next.

**Why grouping still helps.** On the 17th, at your suggestion, we re-dealt the batches that hadn't started. Each batch now holds functions with the same lever type, from the same source file where possible. That pays off in three ways:
- **Similar moves.** Functions with the same lever type tend to fall to the same few moves. In T10, about half the wins came from two tricks: reusing a variable to steer the compiler's choices, and putting a store in each branch of an if instead of using a barrier. A coder that has just cracked a barrier with one of those tricks tries it first on the next barrier.
- **Already-read context.** Functions from the same file share types and headers the coder has already read. Re-reading cached context costs about a tenth of fresh reading, so the coder doesn't pay again to understand the file.
- **Shared notes.** Every coder adds the move that cracked each function, or the wall it hit, to `.run/P40/T11/moves.md`. Every new coder reads that file first, so what one coder learns reaches the others too.

Batches stay at about 5 to 10 functions. Much longer than that, and the coder's old notes start crowding out the function in front of it. For MiniMax we're keeping batches to 5 or fewer, since one of its earlier runs ran out of room.

Yes, m2c was our main first-draft tool all through matching, and it's still a submodule at `tools/m2c`. It just doesn't help T11.

**How we used it.** `tools/decompile.py` runs m2c on a function's disassembly to produce a C draft, optionally given our existing types so its output uses them. Agents started from that draft, or from Ghidra's output if that was closer. Then they edited it until the compiled bytes matched. About ten other tools also call it, including the declaration repair and signature tools.

**"Perfect C for small functions" is half true.** On short, simple functions m2c's draft often matches as-is or after small tweaks. But as functions grow, its drafts drift further from the original. We measured this when building the actor struct (`docs/actor-struct.md`): on functions m2c got structurally wrong, 50 to 98% of the instructions mismatched. Giving it the real struct changed nothing (0 better, 10 the same, 2 worse), because those misses are limits of the decompiler itself, not missing types. It also often drops function arguments. That's partly why T7 found so many pins were really missing parameters.

**Why it can't do T11's work.** Every function in T11 already has correct C that matches. What's left is the last step: getting the same bytes without a pin or barrier. That depends on how gcc 2.7.2 picks registers and orders code. m2c reads the assembly and writes C that means the same thing. It doesn't try spellings and compile them against the target bytes, which is what the coders do. A fresh m2c draft would typically land back at the same wall, or further from it.

I'd expect somewhat better results, but not a big jump. The judge removes friction, not the hard part.

**What the judge and this release fix:**
- **Refused commands.** Before, a command outside the allow rules was simply refused. The coder then wasted turns finding a workaround or did without the tool. Now the judge rules once and the project remembers. In this run alone it has already allowed `objdump` and the scoring script.
- **Runs that die.** Batch G06 failed with "Prompt is too long". MiniMax now saves its progress and hands off to a fresh coder at 350k tokens, so a run like that is no longer lost.
- **Lessons carrying over.** After each run, the expert now corrects its next brief and writes notes for later coders. So later MiniMax coders start knowing what the earlier ones learned.

Together these should mean fewer failed runs and more of each run spent actually trying spellings.

**What they don't fix.** Cracking a singleton comes down to reasoning about how gcc 2.7.2 picks registers and merges copies, then guessing which spelling tips it. In MiniMax's first session, its 10 walls fell on the same compiler behaviours as Haiku's: merged copies and ties in register choice. That points to the model's reasoning, or to real walls, not missing tools. Its clean crack rate was 37%, against Haiku's 57% and Opus's 50 to 60%.

My guess is a few points better, maybe into the 40s, mostly from fewer wasted or failed runs. The comparison also won't be clean. The batches left now include functions earlier coders already tried and failed, so they're harder on average. The expert's report after this first coder will show how much friction the judge removed. Its crack rate over the next few batches will tell us the rest.

T11 is resuming, and it ramps MiniMax up until OpenRouter throttles us.

**The limit.** I raised the MiniMax limit from 4 coders to 10 (commit 3c202bcac5). The machine can take that: it has 32 CPU cores and 26 GB of disk free. That commit also picked up the waiting journal files, which is harmless. Ten is a ceiling, not a target. If the free tier holds at 10 and you want more, say so and I'll raise it.

**How the expert ramps up:**
- **Start and grow.** It starts 4 coders from the batches' handoffs, then adds about 2 at a time while runs stay healthy.
- **Throttling.** On the first rate-limit errors (429s) or runs failing on the provider, it stops adding coders. Failed runs pick up again once a slot frees, and it settles one or two coders below the level that throttled. It logs the level reached, so we'll know MiniMax's real ceiling.
- **Safeguards stay.**
  - Free disk stays above 10 GB.
  - Batches have 5 functions or fewer.
  - Each coder's final message starts with the bare word "done".
  - An Opus coder banks every 6 to 8 finished batches.
  - Walls go to your held list.

One caution: G08c's run used 19.6M tokens for 4 functions. That costs nothing on the free tier, but it's why the rate limit will probably arrive early. I'll tell you the level where it settles.
